clinicalPearls: The commonest recognised genetic cause of Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease, inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion through loss of the shared beta-1 chain of the interleukin-12 and interleukin-23 receptors
Loss of the receptor blunts interferon-gamma production by lymphocytes, weakening defence against intramacrophage organisms
Typical presentation is disseminated BCG disease after vaccination, recurrent non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection, and non-typhoidal Salmonella septicaemia or gastroenteritis
Mucocutaneous or invasive candidiasis can occur because the same receptor drives interleukin-23-dependent T-helper-17 responses that guard mucosal surfaces
Clinical penetrance is incomplete, so some individuals carrying biallelic defects remain healthy or present only in later childhood
Diagnosis is supported by absent surface expression of the receptor beta-1 chain on activated lymphocytes and impaired interferon-gamma production after interleukin-12 stimulation
Most patients respond to prolonged targeted antimicrobial therapy, and prognosis is generally more favourable than for complete interferon-gamma receptor defects
reference.pathophysiology: Interleukin-12 and interleukin-23 share a common receptor beta-1 subunit encoded by IL12RB1, and this subunit is essential for both cytokines to signal into T and natural killer cells. Interleukin-12 signalling drives these lymphocytes to produce interferon-gamma, which then activates macrophages to kill ingested mycobacteria and Salmonella; interleukin-23 signalling supports the maintenance of interleukin-17-producing T cells that protect mucosal surfaces against fungi. When the beta-1 chain is absent, cells cannot respond to either cytokine, interferon-gamma output collapses, and the phagocyte activation loop fails, leaving the host unable to contain weakly virulent intracellular organisms; the accompanying weakness in the interleukin-23/interleukin-17 arm explains the added tendency to candidiasis.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis from STAT1 gain-of-function or other causes
additionalInvestigations: Flow cytometry for surface interleukin-12 receptor beta-1 expression on activated T and natural killer cells
Whole-blood assay of interferon-gamma production after stimulation with interleukin-12 and mycobacterial antigen
Genetic sequencing of IL12RB1 and related MSMD genes
Mycobacterial and Salmonella cultures with species-level identification
Assessment for candidal infection at mucosal and invasive sites
Screening for HIV and other acquired immunodeficiency
redFlags: Progressive or multifocal non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection
Consanguinity with a family history of childhood mycobacterial or Salmonella infection
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is comparatively good among the mycobacterial susceptibility disorders; many patients survive into adulthood with prolonged antimicrobial therapy, although infections may recur and a minority succumb to overwhelming early disease.
pitfalls: Assuming healthy relatives who share the genotype exclude the diagnosis, given incomplete penetrance
Stopping antibiotics prematurely and precipitating relapse
Administering live BCG before the diagnosis is considered in an at-risk family
Overlooking coexistent candidiasis attributable to the interleukin-23 arm
Relying on a normal immunoglobulin and lymphocyte profile to rule out the condition
references: Stiehm's Immunologic Disorders in Infants and Children
IUIS Expert Committee classification of inborn errors of immunity
management: Treat mycobacterial disease and non-typhoidal Salmonella infection with prolonged, culture-directed multidrug antimicrobial therapy
Administer recombinant interferon-gamma as adjunctive therapy, effective because the downstream interferon-gamma receptor and STAT1 pathway are intact
Treat mucocutaneous or invasive candidiasis with antifungals, reflecting the impaired interleukin-23 and interleukin-17 arm
Provide antimicrobial prophylaxis against recurrent infection and avoid live BCG vaccination
Manage disseminated or septicaemic deterioration urgently with blood cultures and directed antimicrobials
Monitor with serial mycobacterial and Salmonella cultures and screen for coexisting acquired immunodeficiency such as HIV
Offer genetic counselling and family screening, noting incomplete penetrance in this autosomal recessive condition
